text.p: New England Electric System Chief Executive John Rowe said Tuesday deregulation will create a "difficult" 1998, but the company is exploring new businesses to ease the transition.

"Restructuring will make 1998 a difficult year and increase the challenge of providing the earnings that you have become used to," Rowe told shareholders at the company's annual meeting in Providence.
Of the 25 bids submitted for New England Electric System's (NEES) 18 non-nuclear electric generating plants up for sale, from four to 10 are serious, he said.
"We're going to get a very attractive price that will help in the transition," Rowe said of the sale.
A select group of the companies will be asked to submit formal, binding bids for the assets, which have a book value of $1.2 billion, by the end of June.
NEES hopes to sign a deal to sell the assets early in the third quarter, he said.
Rowe said NEES will soon announce a joint venture with a telecommunications company which will take advantage of NEES' transmission capabilities.
Rowe did not elaborate on the telecom initiative.

He said that the company is exploring entering the electricity transmission business in Argentina and Brazil. Specifically, the company is examining the possibility of a tranasmission line from Argentina's gas companies to the growing markets in Brazil.
NEES also will seek to expand its electricity transmission capabilities in the New York-New England region, and may also someday get involved in gas transmission, Rowe said.
Rowe said the new businesses will help defray any costs associated with stranded assets, such as its stake in nuclear plants which will be less competitive in a deregulated market.
"We now have the framework for that recovery (of stranded assets) in place," he said.

Rowe estimated the company's stranded assets at $3 billion to $4.5 billion but said that higher figure could come down with the sale of generating assets going well, and increasing demand for electricity.

In response to questions from shareholders, many of whom were seniors, Rowe said the company was committed to awarding good dividends, but he admitted the company's policy may change as the business changes.
"We know dividends are important to you and we are committed to providing good dividends," he said.
